docs.D00_original_thesis.md:
Title: Original investment thesis — January 26 investor letter
Source: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/01/26170421/Pershing-Square-Capital-Management-L.P.-Releases-Letter-to-Investors-01-26-2022.pdf
Date: 2022-01-26

The following short extracts preserve the original underwriting assumptions; intervening explanation is paraphrase. The position was initiated following the January earnings-related price decline, not before it. The letter reports more than 3.1 million shares purchased beginning the preceding Friday. It distinguishes an attractive long-term franchise from disappointing short-term subscriber guidance.

“Netflix is a primary beneficiary of the growth in streaming and the decline in linear TV”

The supporting explanation emphasizes customer experience, continually refreshed content, broadband availability and increasingly convenient viewing devices. This is an industry-transition thesis: streaming gains entertainment share, and Netflix's scale helps it capture the growth. It does not require exclusive ownership of every successful show.

The letter identifies “subscription-based, highly recurring revenues” and “a truly best-in-class management team”. It cites the company's transitions from mailed DVDs to streaming and original production as evidence of adaptability and a high-performance culture. Management credibility is therefore an explicit part of the purchase case, not just an incidental characteristic.

Its moat argument combines content quality and economies of scale. A large subscriber base spreads the cost of programming, while desirable programming attracts and retains subscribers. The pricing argument is “pricing power derived from the enormous value it delivers to consumers compared with other alternatives”.

Two further underwriting pillars are margin expansion as the global subscriber base grows, and improving free cash flow that permits both reinvestment and shareholder distributions. These claims connect revenue growth to per-share intrinsic value; recurring billing alone does not establish recurring cash profit.

The purchase was funded by monetizing most of an interest-rate hedge. The letter reports $1.25 billion of hedge proceeds and says the Netflix investment offered a more compelling risk/reward. That financing history is already public; it does not establish the correct decision now.

The original thesis can be tested against the April results along four independent dimensions: member acquisition and retention; pricing net of churn; content-cost leverage; and conversion of accounting earnings to cash. A revised business model may be sensible but still require a fresh forecast rather than extrapolation of the original subscriber-growth curve.
docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Business, regional economics and governance
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000035/ex991_q421.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm
Date: 2022-04-19

Netflix sells access to an on-demand library of films and television, with a small legacy DVD operation. The subscription is cancellable, so billed recurring revenue is not a long-term customer contract. Producing and licensing programming requires substantial cash before viewing occurs. Content assets are amortized through expenses over their expected useful lives; spending and reported content expense therefore differ.

Reed Hastings and Ted Sarandos are co-CEOs. Sarandos also leads content; Greg Peters is COO and chief product officer, and Spencer Neumann is CFO. Management's January letter proposes declassifying the board, removing supermajority provisions and allowing shareholders to call special meetings. April's letter reiterates that these changes will be presented at the June meeting. They are proposals, not completed changes.

At December 31, 2021, the regional subscription economics were:

| Region | Paid memberships, millions | Q4 revenue, $millions | Monthly revenue per membership |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| US/Canada | 75.22 | 3,309 | $14.78 |
| Europe/Middle East/Africa | 74.04 | 2,523 | $11.64 |
| Latin America | 39.96 | 964 | $8.14 |
| Asia-Pacific | 32.63 | 871 | $9.26 |

Regional revenue is not regional profit. The company does not provide comparable regional operating margins in these earnings letters. Lower local pricing and currency movements make a subscriber in one region economically different from a subscriber elsewhere.

The April letter identifies global content production, personalized presentation and viewing engagement as competitive advantages. Netflix produces in more than 50 countries. Management describes Netflix as the largest subscription streaming service by memberships, engagement, revenue and profit. These are company assertions, not proof that growth remains predictable.

The quarter ended March 31 with 221.64 million paid memberships, down from 221.84 million in December. Management estimates more than 100 million additional households share paying members' accounts, including over 30 million in US/Canada. These are potential monetization targets, not paid subscribers or signed contracts.

Q1 weighted-average diluted shares were 452.984 million, versus 455.795 million in Q4. The share denominator includes dilution and is not an exact period-end outstanding share count. The firm's principal operating leverage runs through content: serving additional viewers costs relatively little at the delivery layer, but keeping the library competitive is not free.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Historical financials and latest-quarter cash economics
Source: compiled from: https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2020/q4/FINAL-Q420-Shareholder-Letter.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000035/ex991_q421.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm
Date: 2022-04-19

The table uses company-reported results, with annual figures in $millions except EPS. Annual values are rounded to the precision shown, not consensus forecasts. The 2019/2020 comparison was public in January 2021; 2021 results were released January 20, 2022.

| Metric | FY2019 | FY2020 | FY2021 | Q1 2022 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 20,156 | 24,996 | 29,698 | 7,868 |
| Operating income | 2,604 | 4,585 | 6,195 | 1,972 |
| Diluted EPS | 4.13 | 6.08 | 11.24 | 3.53 |
| Free cash flow | approximately -3,300 | 1,922 | -159 | 802 |

FY2021 revenue grew 19%; operating income grew 35%. The full-year operating margin was 21%, versus 18% in 2020. Q1 2022 revenue grew 9.8% and operating margin was 25.1%. A strong quarterly margin does not imply an acceleration in underlying demand: management attributes the favorable operating-profit variance partly to content expense arriving below forecast.

FY2021 operating cash flow was $392.610 million. Property/equipment purchases were $524.585 million and changes in other assets used $26.919 million, producing company-defined FCF of negative $158.894 million. Content additions were $17,702.202 million, while content amortization was $12,230.367 million. Consequently, conventional physical capex is a poor measure of the economic reinvestment burden.

At March 31, cash was $6,008.946 million and carrying-value debt was $14,534.561 million. The company's net-debt measure, adding debt issuance costs, was $8,614.244 million. Net debt/LTM adjusted EBITDA was 1.3x. This EBITDA measure retains content amortization; an EBITDA measure adding it back would be economically misleading.

Q1 operating cash flow of $922.839 million less $121.158 million property/equipment purchases yielded FCF of $801.681 million. Acquisitions used another $124.521 million, outside that FCF definition.

Netflix repaid $700 million of notes in Q1 and made no share repurchases. FY2021 cash repurchases were $600.022 million; the treasury-stock balance also reflects equity-award settlement. No dividend is announced in these releases. A consistently defined ROIC series is not supplied. Management still expects positive full-year 2022 FCF, but that expectation is not a realized annual result.
docs.D03_latest_results.md:
Title: April 19 results — subscriber shortfall and a changed growth diagnosis
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm; https://www.cnbc.com/2022/04/19/netflix-is-exploring-lower-priced-ad-supported-plans-after-years-of-resisting.html
Date: 2022-04-19

Q1 revenue was $7,867.767 million, operating income $1,971.626 million and diluted EPS $3.53. January's forecast had called for $7,903 million revenue, $1,765 million operating income and $2.86 EPS. Profit therefore exceeded forecast while the subscriber measure central to the growth model missed materially.

Paid net additions were negative 0.2 million, versus management's positive 2.5 million forecast. Russia's service suspension removed 0.7 million memberships; excluding Russia, additions were positive 0.5 million. Even on that adjusted basis, acquisition was considerably below the original company forecast.

The letter says: “Our revenue growth has slowed considerably”. It no longer attributes the slowdown principally to pandemic pull-forward. Management lists four interacting constraints: broadband/connected-TV adoption and other addressable-market limits; widespread account sharing; streaming competition; and macroeconomic weakness, inflation and geopolitical disruption.

US/Canada lost 0.6 million memberships. Management says the price change is tracking expectations and is “significantly revenue positive”. Latin America lost 0.4 million; Europe/Middle East/Africa lost 0.3 million including Russia. Asia-Pacific remains a source of member growth. Revenue-positive pricing can coexist with falling memberships; neither measure alone resolves long-term customer economics.

For Q2, Netflix forecasts another 2.0 million net subscriber losses. Revenue guidance is $8,053 million, 9.7% growth. The company retains its 19%-20% full-year operating-margin target, assuming no material currency shifts from January levels. It intends to protect profitability near current levels while rebuilding revenue growth, rather than continue automatic annual margin expansion.

The earnings interview also marks a strategic change. CNBC reports Hastings is open to lower-priced, advertising-supported plans, with development over the next year or two. This is exploration, not an operating product with disclosed advertiser demand or measured margins.

The company is also testing paid account-sharing features in three Latin American markets. Management views the non-paying audience as an opportunity, but acknowledges it cannot monetize all sharing immediately. Neither advertising economics nor conversion/churn from account enforcement is quantified. A forecast now needs explicit assumptions for both initiatives, not simply a new subscriber count.
docs.D04_price_valuation.md:
Title: April 20 price shock and valuation limits
Source: compiled from: https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/story/2022-04-20/lat-et-ct-netflix-stock-plunges; https://www.cnbc.com/2022/01/24/netflix-shares-fall-to-lowest-since-april-2020-on-subscriber-concern.html; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm
Date: 2022-04-20

The Los Angeles Times reports an April 20 close of $226.19, down 35.1% in one session following the first-quarter subscriber loss. This replay uses the closing price, so it is an end-of-day analytical snapshot rather than an intraday execution simulation. It excludes any manager decision announcement.

CNBC's January 24 article recorded a $387.15 close on that date and said Netflix traded above $700 in November. Comparing $226.19 with $700 indicates a decline exceeding 67%; that is a reference-level comparison, not a fully verified 52-week high/low series.

Using reported FY2021 EPS of $11.24 gives a trailing P/E of 20.1x, calculated as $226.19/$11.24. Replacing Q1 2021 EPS of $3.75 with Q1 2022 EPS of $3.53 gives a simple rolling-EPS proxy of $11.02 and a 20.5x multiple. This proxy does not recompute changing diluted-share denominators and is not a vendor-certified trailing P/E.

Using Q1 basic weighted-average shares of 444.146 million gives illustrative equity capitalization of $100.46 billion. Adding the company's $8.614 billion net-debt measure gives an illustrative enterprise value of $109.08 billion. Dividing by reported $6.869 billion LTM adjusted EBITDA yields about 15.9x. These are explicit calculations using a quarterly average share count, not exact closing market capitalization or a consensus enterprise multiple.

The FY2021 free-cash-flow yield is negative, since reported FCF was negative. Annualizing the seasonally strong Q1 cash result is not an appropriate normalized yield. No reliable timestamped forward EPS consensus, forecast EPS growth, five-to-ten-year forward-multiple range, S&P 500 forward multiple, complete 52-week range or April 20 volume was recovered from the cited sources. Those figures are not supplied as substitutes from memory.

The share is substantially cheaper on trailing earnings than before the price shock. Whether it is cheap on prospective owner earnings depends on subscriber retention, content spending and the economics of the proposed business-model changes. A falling multiple does not by itself establish a wider margin of safety when the earnings distribution also changes.
docs.D05_market_concerns.md:
Title: Contemporary bear case — saturation, competition and monetization risk
Source: compiled from: https://www.reuters.com/technology/netflix-subscribers-fall-first-time-decade-forecasts-more-losses-2022-04-19; https://www.cnbc.com/2022/04/19/netflix-nflx-earnings-q1-2022.html; https://www.cnbc.com/2022/04/19/netflix-is-exploring-lower-priced-ad-supported-plans-after-years-of-resisting.html
Date: 2022-04-20

Reuters' April 19 report, updated April 20, describes inflation, the Ukraine war and fierce competition as contributors to Netflix's subscriber loss. CNBC's April 19 earnings report contrasts negative 200,000 net additions with StreetAccount expectations for positive 2.73 million. These are separately dated market expectations, not the company's January guidance of positive 2.5 million.

The principal concern is that the highly penetrated core market no longer supports the acquisition curve investors used to justify large content commitments. Russia explains part of the reported decline, but excluding it does not restore the expected growth. The Q2 forecast for another two million losses challenges a one-quarter explanation.

The company's own April letter says the pandemic obscured the growth problem. That is more consequential than a single miss because it changes how prior data should be interpreted: pandemic subscriber additions may have pulled future demand forward, while competition and account sharing independently constrain conversion.

Competition acts at several levels. Disney+, HBO Max and other services compete for subscriptions and programming. YouTube and other entertainment compete for time. Households may maintain multiple services, but a discretionary budget limits pricing freedom and increases churn risk. Netflix's content scale is an advantage, not immunity from an escalating programming bill.

CNBC reports the reversal of Hastings' resistance to advertising. A lower-priced ad tier could expand the audience, but it could also draw existing full-price subscribers into a cheaper plan. Advertising sales, measurement, technology and revenue sharing create economic variables absent from a pure-subscription extrapolation. No operating history for that tier is available in this snapshot.

Paid-sharing enforcement similarly offers possible revenue without new content, yet the conversion rate is unknown. A non-paying household can subscribe, stop watching or remain difficult to identify. The 100-million-household estimate is not a receivable.

These concerns do not establish that Netflix is a poor company. The immediate underwriting question is whether its long-run revenue, margins and cash needs can still be estimated tightly enough for a concentrated position. The distinction between business quality and forecast confidence is essential: an apparently lower price can accompany both a compelling recovery opportunity and a much wider range of plausible intrinsic values.
docs.D06_peers_industry.md:
Title: Streaming competitors and the limits of subscriber comparisons
Source: compiled from: https://s206.q4cdn.com/979796730/files/doc_events/2021/11/q4-fy21-earnings.pdf; https://www.reuters.com/markets/europe/hbo-max-shows-growth-despite-industry-slowdown-2022-01-05; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000035/ex991_q421.htm; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm
Date: 2022-04-19

The available dated comparisons describe two major competitors. The Disney figures below are deliberately the older November release, not a claim that they represent Disney's latest April subscriber count. They provide a verified pre-cutoff economic benchmark. A fully synchronized peer-valuation table is not available in the retrieved sources.

| Company/service | Observation date | Scale and economics |
|---|---|---|
| Netflix | January 20, FY2021 results | 221.84m year-end members; 21% operating margin; $29.698bn revenue |
| Disney+ | November 10, FY2021 release | 118.1m members; 60% year-on-year growth |
| Disney direct-to-consumer | November 10, fiscal Q4 release | $4.6bn quarterly revenue; $630m operating loss |
| HBO/HBO Max | January 5 public update | 73.8m combined year-end subscribers, versus 69.4m in September |
| Netflix | April 19, Q1 results | 221.64m members; 25.1% quarterly operating margin |

Disney's DTC segment includes Hulu and ESPN+ as well as Disney+. Its loss cannot be assigned entirely to Disney+, and a Disney+ subscription is not necessarily equivalent to a full-priced Netflix subscription. Likewise, HBO/HBO Max's combined count includes the traditional premium network as well as streaming. These definitions matter when using scale to infer programming economics.

The industry offers relatively low distribution costs but high and continuing content investment. A program can be watched globally without reproducing physical inventory, supporting operating leverage. Yet subscriptions can be cancelled readily, and competing libraries reduce the exclusivity of any one service's entertainment offering.

Netflix's advantage is demonstrated current profitability and a large global base over which to spread content expense. The peer evidence also shows that rivals can sustain losses while investing in subscriber acquisition, especially inside diversified parent companies. A profitable incumbent need not win every incremental household to create value; equally, industry growth does not guarantee rising margins for every provider.

Peer P/E and EV/EBITDA figures are omitted: parent-company valuation mixes parks, linear networks, telecom or other businesses with streaming, and timestamped segment multiples were not recovered. Comparisons should therefore focus on disclosed operating economics and definitions rather than imply false precision from incomparable headline subscriber totals.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Dated timeline through the April results
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000035/ex991_q421.htm; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/01/26170421/Pershing-Square-Capital-Management-L.P.-Releases-Letter-to-Investors-01-26-2022.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm; https://www.cnbc.com/2022/04/19/netflix-is-exploring-lower-priced-ad-supported-plans-after-years-of-resisting.html
Date: 2022-04-19

**2021:** Netflix added about 18 million paid memberships, versus about 37 million in 2020. The January earnings letter reports this comparison. The slowdown provides essential context for distinguishing pandemic normalization from a more durable acquisition problem.

**Late 2021:** Squid Game demonstrated the global appeal of locally produced programming. Netflix's January letter reports 1.65 billion viewing hours during its first four weeks. The Roald Dahl Story Company acquisition was funded from cash during Q4. These developments support content reach and intellectual-property ownership, but require capital allocation rather than prove subscriber growth by themselves.

**December 2021:** Netflix lowered prices across its four plans in India. January's letter says low local pay-TV prices make India unusual, and that the goal is maximizing long-run revenue in each market. This is a useful counterweight to a universal-pricing-power thesis.

**January 20, 2022:** Q4 results showed 8.28 million paid net additions, slightly below the 8.5 million forecast. Q1 guidance was only 2.5 million. Management targeted 19%-20% 2022 operating margin, compared with 21% in 2021, in part because of dollar strength.

**January 21-26:** The manager's January 26 letter publicly describes purchases beginning January 21 and a holding exceeding 3.1 million shares. It emphasizes recurring revenues, management, content scale, pricing power, margins and improving cash generation. This is information already public for the existing-position replay.

**March 2022:** Netflix introduced paid-sharing features in three Latin American markets. The April letter dates this launch and describes it as part of tests started earlier. It has not supplied a mature financial record for the initiative.

**Q1 2022:** Suspension and winding-down of Russian subscriptions reduced paid memberships by 0.7 million. The April letter separates this effect from the underlying acquisition shortfall.

**April 19:** Results show negative 0.2 million net additions and guide to negative 2.0 million in Q2. Hastings discusses exploring an advertising-supported tier over one to two years. These are distinct changes: current subscriber performance, a deteriorating near-term forecast, and an unproven future monetization strategy. No subsequent operating results are included.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: Portfolio concentration, investment standards and financing context
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/03/29140526/Pershing-Square-Holdings-Ltd.-2021-Annual-Report.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/01/26170421/Pershing-Square-Capital-Management-L.P.-Releases-Letter-to-Investors-01-26-2022.pdf
Date: 2022-03-29

The March 29 annual report provides a portfolio overview already public before the April results. It describes approximately 30% of the equity portfolio in music/video streaming, comprising Universal Music Group and Netflix; 26% in restaurants and franchising, comprising Chipotle, Restaurant Brands and Domino's; 15% in home improvement through Lowe's; with Hilton, Canadian Pacific and Howard Hughes representing other principal exposures. These are category/manager descriptions, not reconstructed daily NAV weights.

The distinction between UMG and Netflix matters. Both benefit from digital distribution and recurring consumption, but music-rights licensing and subscription-video production have different content economics. A favorable view of streaming as a category does not establish an identical predictability standard for each holding.

In January, purchases of more than 3.1 million Netflix shares were funded by $1.25 billion of proceeds from unwinding most of the interest-rate hedge. That letter says the notional hedge was reduced by 80%, its dollar investment by more than 90%, while some longer-dated out-of-the-money protection remained. Those historical proceeds are not April 20 uncommitted cash.

The January 26 letter states: “We invest in hedges not to protect the funds from a short-term mark-to-market loss”. It instead describes hedges as potential liquidity when stocks become cheap, structured to limit losses if the anticipated risk does not occur. This supports evaluating opportunity cost and prospective risk/reward rather than defending an earlier purchase mechanically.

The same letter says many attractive investments arise when short-horizon investors discard great companies. That philosophy supports tolerating volatility when intrinsic-value assumptions remain intact; it does not say every decline warrants adding capital. Management quality, recurring revenue, scale economics, pricing power and cash generation were the explicit Netflix purchase criteria.

A precise April 20 manager-wide AUM, same-day cash balance and each security's current weight are not supplied in these extracts. PSH is one listed fund, while manager-wide holdings span multiple vehicles; 13F equity totals would omit cash, derivatives and foreign holdings. These distinctions prevent a false precision in position sizing. The portfolio context is concentrated ownership of a few businesses, not an index-like allocation that can ignore a widening range of outcomes in one major holding.
docs.D09_changes_since_purchase.md:
Title: Original assumptions compared with information now available
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/01/26170421/Pershing-Square-Capital-Management-L.P.-Releases-Letter-to-Investors-01-26-2022.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528022000144/ex991_q122.htm; https://www.cnbc.com/2022/04/19/netflix-is-exploring-lower-priced-ad-supported-plans-after-years-of-resisting.html
Date: 2022-04-19

The January purchase case assumed a high-quality subscription business facing disappointing short-term growth. The current information must be separated into evidence confirming that case, evidence weakening it, and variables not yet measurable. The purpose is a fresh underwriting decision, not a conclusion dictated by the investment's purchase price.

**Evidence that remains favorable:** Netflix is profitable, has global production capabilities and substantial viewing engagement. Q1 operating profit exceeded January guidance. Reported price changes remain revenue-positive, and management still forecasts positive 2022 FCF. The company has reduced gross debt and reports only 1.3x net leverage under its stated adjusted EBITDA definition.

**Evidence that has deteriorated:** Q1 memberships fell rather than rising 2.5 million. Russia explains 0.7 million removals, but the ex-Russia result still falls materially short. The company forecasts a further two million subscriber losses. January's explanation emphasized pandemic pull-forward and slow acquisition; April's explanation explicitly adds household penetration, account sharing and competition as significant barriers.

**A changed margin pathway:** The original letter emphasized substantial margin expansion from scale. Management now plans to hold margin roughly around current levels while attempting to restore growth. Lower subscriber growth spreads programming costs over fewer incremental payers. Current profitability therefore does not settle the trajectory of future profitability.

**A changed monetization model:** Advertising and paid sharing may create value, but their unit economics are not yet disclosed. An ad tier introduces advertiser demand, sales costs, viewing mix and possible subscription cannibalization. Account-sharing enforcement introduces conversion and churn uncertainty. Neither opportunity can be valued simply by treating all non-paying households as future full-price members.

**What is not established:** There is no disclosed, tested ad-tier margin; no robust conversion curve for paid sharing; and no demonstrated timetable for restoring the prior subscriber-growth rate. The price shock alone does not fill these gaps.

The analytical alternatives are to underwrite a conservative growth path using established subscription economics, explicitly model new business lines with wide ranges, or conclude that the range is too broad for the portfolio's concentration. A credible management team can still face an outcome distribution that differs substantially from the one assumed at purchase. This comparison deliberately supplies no manager decision.

drivers.driver: Subscriber-growth changes have an outsized effect on intrinsic value because of operating leverage.
drivers.quote: changes in the company’s future subscriber growth can have an outsized impact on our estimate of intrinsic value

drivers.driver: Advertising and account-sharing changes may be sensible but are difficult to forecast.
drivers.quote: it is extremely difficult to predict their impact on the company’s long-term subscriber growth, future revenues, operating margins, and capital intensity

drivers.driver: The business no longer meets the predictability requirement for a concentrated core holding.
drivers.quote: we have lost confidence in our ability to predict the company’s future prospects with a sufficient degree of certainty

drivers.driver: Act promptly when new evidence contradicts the original thesis.
drivers.quote: One of our learnings from past mistakes is to act promptly when we discover new information about an investment that is inconsistent with our original thesis.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: Ten documents including original-thesis and changes-since-purchase documents. Same-day exit letter completely excluded from pack. Latest peer synchronized multiples, exact AUM/cash, 52-week range, forward consensus and volume not recovered. Equity/EV proxies explicitly use quarterly average shares. Meta AUM null means unavailable, not zero. Some documents below the preferred 300-word floor; no padding.

thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: Subscription-based, highly recurring revenues: broken/weakened by subscriber loss and guidance of further declines [D04], [D06]
Predictable subscriber growth/streaming beneficiary: broken; management cited new constraints including penetration, competition, and account sharing [D04], [D06]
Margin expansion as global subscriber base grows: broken; management now expects to hold margins steady rather than expand [D04], [D10]
Best-in-class management: intact; management is taking proactive, if unproven, strategic steps to address the growth slowdown [D02], [D04], [D10]
final.valuation_now: The stock trades at ~20x trailing EPS [D05], but the earnings growth trajectory is highly uncertain due to shifting business model drivers [D04], [D06]

drivers.driver: The fundamental growth thesis has changed, leading to a loss of predictability in the company's core subscription model [D04], [D06].

final.memo:
Our investment in the Company was predicated on a thesis of predictable, recurring, high-margin subscriber growth, underpinned by a dominant streaming franchise and best-in-class management [D00]. The Q1 results and the forward guidance of further subscriber losses fundamentally challenge this core underwriting [D04]. The company has moved from a predictable growth trajectory to one where the management must now explore unproven initiatives—namely advertising-supported tiers and paid-account sharing—to compensate for saturation and competitive pressure [D04], [D06], [D10].

While management remains high-quality and the business remains profitable, the shift away from an automatic, scale-driven margin expansion path reduces the predictability of our long-term earnings forecast [D02], [D04], [D10]. Our standards require that we be able to forecast a business's free-cash-flow generation with sufficient certainty to justify a concentrated position; we can no longer do so here until these new monetization models are tested and the subscriber churn stabilizes [D00], [D06], [D10]. 

We do not hold positions when the business model or its drivers have changed to the extent that we can no longer forecast with confidence [D00]. Consequently, we are exiting the position today, notwithstanding the significant decline in the stock price, as we must prioritize capital allocation to opportunities that fit our strict quality and predictability criteria [D05], [D06], [D10].

thesis_at_purchase_vs_now: pricing power: weakened by competition and budget constraints [D06]
final.valuation_now: multiple is lower at 20.1x trailing earnings [D05], but prospective earnings range is too wide [D06]

drivers.driver: The core growth thesis has deteriorated due to unforeseen subscriber losses and a fundamental change in our ability to forecast future revenue and margin expansion.

final.memo:
We invest in simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, dominant businesses [D00]. When we purchased Netflix, our thesis rested on the company being a primary beneficiary of the streaming transition, underpinned by highly predictable subscription-based, recurring revenues and significant operating leverage [D00]. We identified a best-in-class management team capable of navigating this growth, with the expectation of consistent margin expansion as the global subscriber base scaled [D00].

However, the results reported on April 19 indicate a material change in the business model's predictability [D04]. With paid net additions falling into negative territory and management guiding for further losses in the second quarter, our original growth trajectory is no longer valid [D04], [D08]. The company's explicit pivot from a pure-subscription model toward unproven advertising-supported plans and account-sharing enforcement introduces new operational variables that we cannot forecast with the required certainty [D04], [D06], [D10].

While management remains high-quality, the range of plausible intrinsic values has widened significantly due to these structural uncertainties [D02], [D06], [D10]. Our standard requires businesses where we can identify the long-run revenue and margin drivers [D00]. Because we can no longer model these with sufficient confidence, we have reached a loss of predictability that necessitates an immediate exit, regardless of the recent price decline [D06], [D10].
